n: Every seventh year was a “release” — a fresh start. It matched the sabbath year when fields rested, giving the poor a regular way out of debt.

f.g: Hebrew shemittah — a letting go or cancellation.

n: Lenders had to cancel (or at least suspend) debts owed by fellow Israelites. It was called “the Lord’s release” because he commanded it and stood behind it.
Foreign traders, who were not part of the covenant community or the sabbath-year system, could still be asked to repay. The release was for fellow Israelites.

f.g: A non-Israelite merchant or traveler, different from the resident “stranger.”

n: God’s ideal: there should be no poor among his people, because his blessing would be generous and the people would share it.

f.w: there shall be no poor among you

n: That ideal depended on faithful obedience. A Zion society is built by people who keep God’s commandments.
A faithful Israel would be a lender, not a borrower — economically secure and independent among the nations.

f.w: thou shalt lend unto many nations

n: When a fellow Israelite was in need, the wealthy must not harden their hearts or clench their fists.

f.w: nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother

n: Instead, open the hand wide and lend enough to truly meet the need.
A warning against calculated stinginess: refusing to lend because the release year is near and the loan would be canceled. God hears the cry of the poor.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for being stingy or grudging.

f.w: he cry unto the LORD against thee

n: Give willingly, without resentment. Generosity opens the way for God’s blessings on everything you do.

f.w: thine heart shall not be grieved

n: Poverty would always exist in a fallen world, so generosity must always continue. Jesus echoed this verse.

f.w: the poor shall never cease out of the land

n: Israelites who sold themselves into service because of debt had to be freed after six years. Servitude among God’s people was meant to be temporary.

f.w: in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free

n: A freed servant must not leave empty-handed.

f.w: thou shalt not let him go away empty

n: Give generously from livestock, grain, and wine so the freed person can make a new start.

f.g: Literally “put a necklace on him” — load him with gifts.
The threshing floor, where grain was processed.

n: The reason: remember you were slaves in Egypt and God set you free. Israel’s past shaped how they treated others.

f.w: thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt

n: Some servants might love the household and choose to stay permanently.

f.w: because he is well with thee
f.g: Because he is happy and well treated with you.

n: A ceremony at the doorpost marked lifelong service: the servant’s ear was pierced with an awl. Some see in it a picture of willing, loving service to the Master.

f.g: A sharp tool for punching holes in leather.

n: Releasing servants shouldn’t feel like a loss — they gave six years of work worth twice a hired laborer’s, and God promises to bless the giver.

f.g: Their service cost half what hiring workers would have.

n: Firstborn male animals belonged to God. They could not be put to work or sheared for wool.
Each year the family ate the firstborn animals in a sacred meal at the sanctuary.

f.w: year by year in the place which the LORD shall choose

n: Animals with defects could not be sacrificed. God deserves our best, a principle fulfilled in Christ, the unblemished Lamb.
A blemished firstborn could be eaten at home as ordinary food by anyone, like game.

f.w: as the roebuck, and as the hart

n: But the blood rule always applied: drain it onto the ground.

f.w: pour it upon the ground as water
